stem: \(\underline{\text{Except for few days}}\) \(\underline{\text{in a year during the monsoon}}\) \(\underline{\text{the river cannot flow on its own}}\) No error
optB: in a year during the monsoon
optC: the river cannot flow on its own
solution: 'few days' needs the article: it should be 'a few days' (a few = some; few = almost none, which reverses the intended meaning). Matches option A.

stem: \(\underline{\text{Being apprised with our approach}}\) \(\underline{\text{the whole neighbourhood}}\) \(\underline{\text{came out to meet the minister}}\) No error
optC: came out to meet the minister
solution: The idiom is 'apprised OF', not 'apprised with'. Matches option A.

stem: \(\underline{\text{The celebrated grammarian Patanjali}}\) \(\underline{\text{was}}\) \(\underline{\text{a contemporary to Pushyamitra Sunga}}\) No error
solution: The correct preposition is 'contemporary OF', not 'contemporary to'. Matches option C.

stem: \(\underline{\text{In spite of repeated warnings}}\) \(\underline{\text{he did not pay heed}}\) \(\underline{\text{to the advices given by the authorities}}\) No error
optC: to the advices given by the authorities
solution: 'Advice' is an uncountable noun and has no plural 'advices'; it should be 'the advice given'. Matches option C.

stem: \(\underline{\text{Buddhism teaches that}}\) \(\underline{\text{freedom from desires}}\) \(\underline{\text{will lead to escape suffering}}\) No error
solution: After 'lead to' a gerund is required: 'will lead to escaping suffering' (or 'freedom from suffering'). Matches option C.

stem: \(\underline{\text{This hardly won liberty}}\) \(\underline{\text{was not to be}}\) \(\underline{\text{lightly abandoned}}\) No error
solution: 'hardly won' (barely/scarcely) is wrong; the intended word is 'hard-won liberty' (won with great difficulty). Matches option A.

stem: \(\underline{\text{With a population of over one billion,}}\) \(\underline{\text{India is second most populous country}}\) \(\underline{\text{in the world after China}}\) No error
optA: With a population of over one billion,
optB: India is second most populous country
solution: A superlative needs the definite article: 'India is THE second most populous country'. Matches option B.

stem: \(\underline{\text{There are hundred of superstitions}}\) \(\underline{\text{which survive}}\) \(\underline{\text{in the various parts of the country}}\) No error
optC: in the various parts of the country
solution: The idiom is 'hundreds of' (indefinite large number takes the plural -s), not 'hundred of'. Matches option A.

stem: \(\underline{\text{Each one}}\) \(\underline{\text{of these chairs}}\) \(\underline{\text{are broken}}\) No error
solution: 'Each one' is singular, so the verb must be singular: 'is broken', not 'are broken'. Matches option C.

stem: \(\underline{\text{India won}}\) \(\underline{\text{by an innings}}\) \(\underline{\text{and three runs}}\) No error
solution: 'won by an innings and three runs' is the correct cricket idiom and the sentence is grammatically sound. Matches option D.

stem: I made them cleaning the room thoroughly.
solution: The causative 'make' takes a bare infinitive: 'I made them clean the room'. Matches option A.

stem: She availed of the big discounts at the sale.
solution: 'Avail' is used reflexively: 'She availed herself of the big discounts'. Matches option D.

stem: When we arrived at Jhansi station, we are keeping our luggages in the cloak room.
solution: The main clause must be past tense to agree with 'arrived', and 'luggage' is uncountable (no 'luggages'): 'we kept our luggage'. Matches option C.

stem: You have finished your work, have you?
solution: A positive statement takes a negative question tag: 'You have finished your work, haven't you?'. Matches option A.

stem: He waits to you for about two hours.
solution: An action continuing over a period takes the present perfect continuous, and the correct preposition is 'for you': 'He has been waiting for you for about two hours'. Matches option D.

stem: 'Boarder' and 'Border'

stem: She hardly speaks to anyone, ______ ?
solution: 'Hardly' makes the statement negative in sense, so the question tag is positive: 'does she?'. Matches option A.

stem: He used to live in Delhi, ______ ?
solution: 'Used to' forms its tag with 'did': the positive statement takes the negative tag 'didn't he?'. Matches option B.

stem: I am late again, ______ ?
solution: The accepted tag for 'I am' is 'aren't I?'. Matches option A.

stem: I suppose you know the answer, ______ ?
solution: With an introductory 'I suppose/think', the tag agrees with the subordinate clause 'you know', giving the negative tag 'don't you?'. Matches option C.

stem: Everyone was informed about the change, ______ ?
solution: 'Everyone' is referred back to by the plural 'they', and the positive statement takes a negative tag: 'weren't they?'. Matches option B.

stem: “Fabian policy”
solution: A 'Fabian policy' (after Fabius the Delayer) is a policy of cautious delay and avoiding decisive action. Matches option B.

stem: “Get someone’s goat”
optD: To explain in a very clear way
solution: 'Get someone's goat' means to irritate or annoy someone. Matches option B.

stem: “Face up to”
solution: 'Face up to' means to confront and accept a difficult situation. Matches option B.

stem: “Held in camera”
solution: 'In camera' means in private, not open to the public (a legal term for a closed hearing). Matches option C.

stem: “Get your walking papers”
solution: 'Get your walking papers' means to be dismissed or fired from a job. Matches option B.

context: One simple physical concept lies behind the formation of the stars: gravitational instability. The concept is not new. Newton first perceived it late in the 17th Century. Imagine a uniform, static cloud of gas in space. Imagine then that the gas is somehow disturbed so that one small spherical region becomes a little denser than the gas around it so that the small region's gravitational field becomes slightly stronger. It now attracts more matter to it and its gravity increases further, causing it to begin to contract. As it contracts its density increases which increases its gravity even more so that it picks up even more matter and contracts even further. The process continues until the small region of gas finally forms a gravitationally bound object.
stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to:
optC: depict successive stages of a phenomenon
optD: demonstrate the evolution of the meaning of a term
solution: The passage traces star formation step by step — disturbance, increasing density, growing gravity, contraction, bound object — i.e. successive stages of a phenomenon. Matches option C.

stem: We quickly established a \(\underline{\text{rapport}}\), and it fell to me to tell him his diagnosis.
solution: 'Rapport' means a close, harmonious relationship or accord. Matches option A.

stem: It would be too dismal for Gwynne to roam through the \(\underline{\text{purlieus}}\) with a policeman.
solution: 'Purlieus' means the outskirts, environs or bordering areas of a place. Matches option D.

stem: Living hidden away in the mountains suited his \(\underline{\text{ascetic}}\) character.
solution: 'Ascetic' means severely self-disciplined and abstinent — austere. Matches option D.

stem: The \(\underline{\text{atheist}}\) wrote a novel disproving the existence of a higher power.
solution: An 'atheist' is one who disbelieves in the existence of God — a disbeliever. Matches option A.

stem: He is a tight-fisted, \(\underline{\text{penurious}}\) boss whose wage scale is well below other bandleaders.
solution: 'Penurious' (reinforced by 'tight-fisted') means unwilling to spend money — miserly. Matches option A.

stem: It has been to start a \(\underline{\text{scurrilous}}\) attack on all his opponents.
solution: 'Scurrilous' means grossly abusive or defamatory; its opposite is respectful praise — admiration ('scandalous' is a synonym). Matches option B.

stem: He succumbed to \(\underline{\text{ennui}}\) and despair.
solution: 'Ennui' is a feeling of listless boredom; its opposite is excitement. Matches option C.

stem: He gave a \(\underline{\text{slapdash}}\) performance.
solution: 'Slapdash' means done hastily and carelessly; its opposite is careful ('hasty' and 'haphazard' are synonyms). Matches option A.

stem: The possibility of success was \(\underline{\text{chimerical}}\).
solution: 'Chimerical' means fanciful, imaginary or impossible; its opposite is feasible. Matches option B.

stem: The policy was criticized for promoting \(\underline{\text{obscurantism}}\) rather than informed debate.
solution: 'Obscurantism' is the practice of deliberately preventing knowledge or understanding; its opposite is enlightenment. Matches option C.
